# Use Perplexity to Prep for a Job Interview — A Step-by-Step Guide

> **In short:** Perplexity is an AI answer engine that searches the web and cites each fact with a clickable link — perfect for interview research. Five focused questions are usually enough to learn what the company does, what's been in the news, and what the role actually involves day to day.

By the end of this guide you'll have a small, focused research file on any company and any role — built in around 20 minutes — plus three rehearsed answers you can actually say out loud. It's for anyone with an interview coming up who doesn't have time to read ten blog posts about the company.

## Before you start
- A Perplexity account. The free plan is enough for this exercise; the paid Pro plan just unlocks more "Pro Search" runs per day. Check Perplexity's site for the current plan details.
- A browser or the Perplexity mobile app — both work the same way for this guide.
- The name of the company you're interviewing with, the exact job title, and ideally the job description copied to your clipboard.
- About 20–30 minutes total. Most of that is reading, not typing.

One honest note up front: Perplexity is great at pulling public information from the web, but it can't read job postings hidden behind a login wall, and it can't tell you exactly what one specific interviewer will ask. Think of it as a research assistant, not a mind reader.

## Step 1 — Open Perplexity and ask what the company does
Open perplexity.ai in a browser, or open the Perplexity mobile app. You'll see a big search box in the middle of the screen with a small **Focus** dropdown underneath and a **Pro Search** button nearby. Leave Focus on "All" and skip Pro Search for this first question. Type a focused, scoped question about the company and press Enter. Perplexity pauses briefly, then writes back a paragraph-style answer with tiny numbered markers beside key claims — click those markers to verify each source. A list of all sources sits at the bottom of the answer.

If your screen looks different — phone layouts shift around between iOS and Android — just look for a single central search bar. That's where you type.

💬 Example: "What does Stripe do, who are its main customers, and how is it different from PayPal and Adyen?"

You'll know it worked when a paragraph appears with superscript numbers next to key claims and a Sources list of roughly 5–10 links below it.

## Step 2 — Find out what's been in the news and what employees say
Stay in the same Perplexity window — it keeps your earlier question as context, so this works like a conversation. Ask a follow-up about recent news and about what employees say about working there. Perplexity searches again, this time pulling from news sites, LinkedIn, and review platforms like Glassdoor. Read the answer, then click at least one of the numbered sources to spot-check a claim.

If the answer feels thin on culture, look for the Focus dropdown and switch it to **Social** — that pulls more from social-media and review-style sites.

💬 Example: "What has Stripe announced in the past 6 months — funding rounds, product launches, leadership changes? And what do employees say about working there?"

You'll know it worked when you have 3–5 concrete facts you could drop naturally into the interview — a recent product, a quoted value, a new leader, a Glassdoor score.

## Step 3 — Learn what the role actually involves day to day
Still in the same chat, ask Perplexity what someone in this role actually does and which skills the typical posting emphasizes. If you have the real job description, paste it in first — pasting the text gives Perplexity much more to work with than just the job title. Perplexity returns a short list of skills plus a typical-day description.

If you only have the job title, you can still ask — just expect a slightly more generic answer.

💬 Example: "Here's the job description for the Senior Product Designer role at Stripe: [paste the posting here]. What does the day-to-day look like, and which 4–6 skills should I be ready to talk about?"

You'll know it worked when you have a short checklist of the skills this role is likely to test in the interview.

## Step 4 — Predict the likely interview questions
Ask Perplexity to switch hats and act as a recruiter for this specific company. Tell it the role, the company, and the skill list from Step 3, then request 8–10 likely questions split into three buckets: behavioral, role-specific craft, and culture-fit. For each question, ask for a one-sentence hint about what a strong answer includes. Perplexity returns a clean numbered list you can copy into a notes app.

If the questions come back sounding generic, ask Perplexity to anchor them to the 4–6 skills you uncovered in Step 3.

💬 Example: "Act as a hiring manager at Stripe interviewing a Senior Product Designer. Give me 10 likely interview questions split into behavioral, craft, and culture-fit. For each, write one sentence on what a strong answer covers."

You'll know it worked when you have 8–10 distinct questions, each with a hint about what the interviewer is really trying to learn.

## Step 5 — Rehearse your three hardest answers out loud
Open the list from Step 4 and pick the three questions that scare you most. Type a draft answer into the same chat and ask Perplexity to (a) cut filler, (b) flag anything vague, and (c) suggest one concrete story, number, or example that would make the answer stick. Read the rewrite out loud. Aim for 60–90 seconds when spoken. Iterate twice if needed — most good answers need at least two passes.

If typing feels slow, the mobile app supports voice input. Speak your answer instead and Perplexity will transcribe it and respond.

💬 Example: "Here's my draft answer to 'Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate': [paste your answer]. Cut filler, flag anything vague, and suggest one concrete detail that would make it stick. Keep it under 90 seconds spoken."

You'll know it worked when you have three rehearsed answers you can deliver out loud without sounding like you're reading from a script.

## Common mistakes
- **Asking one giant question.** "Tell me everything about Stripe" returns a surface skim. The fix: split it into the four focused questions from Steps 1–3 — what it does, what's in the news, the role, and likely questions.
- **Trusting citations without clicking.** Perplexity cites its sources, but the linked article sometimes only partially backs up the claim. The fix: click any citation that surprises you and glance at the original.
- **Memorizing your rehearsed answer word for word.** It shows in your delivery. The fix: use the rewritten answers as a skeleton — the keywords, the one story, the one number — and let the actual words come out naturally in the room.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** any big personal decision — a vacation, a school choice, a major purchase — benefits from the same pattern. Scope a question, sharpen it with a follow-up, click a source to verify.
- **For your work:** pre-meeting research, vendor due diligence, and quick competitive analysis all use the same Perplexity flow, just with different prompts.
- **If you're just getting started:** pick any company you already buy from or follow (your employer, a favorite brand, a competitor) and ask Perplexity: "What are the three biggest news stories about [company] this week?" That's your first muscle movement.

## Try it now
Pick the company you're interviewing with. Open Perplexity. Type the Step 1 example word for word — replace "Stripe" with your company's name. In about a minute you'll know more than half the other candidates walking into that room.
